title: Fit a yoke regulator onto a portable oxygen cylinder's pin-index valve, hand-tight
instruction: Fit the regulator onto the oxygen cylinder's valve, hand-tight and ready to use, and let go of it.
context: More than 1.5 million adults in the US use supplemental oxygen at home (American Thoracic Society workshop report, Ann Am Thorac Soc 2018). A portable cylinder is what lets them leave the house, but every fresh cylinder needs its regulator fitted. Many users have limited hand strength or dexterity, so they wait for a family caregiver or a supplier's visit, or go without oxygen when out. A robot that can do this reliably helps them stay independent. The yoke slides over the valve post, and its two Pin Index Safety System pins must drop into the valve's two oxygen holes, which the yoke hides. Then the T-handle is turned until it clamps the valve against the sealing washer. A yoke that is not seated on its pins, or is left loose, leaks oxygen. One hand holds the yoke square on its pins while the other turns the screw through several regrips.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Cylinder: an empty size D aluminium medical oxygen cylinder (111 mm diameter, 419 mm from neck ring to base, green shoulder, about 2.4 kg with its valve), lying along x with its axis 12.25 cm above the table. Its brass CGA 870 pin-index post valve points at the robot: the post is a 25 x 28 mm block 60 mm long (free end at x = 0.274, on the cylinder's axis), with a 6 mm square spindle end on its free end and a 3 mm 45-degree chamfer along the free end's top and bottom edges, joined to the shoulder by a 25 mm long, 25 mm diameter neck. The outlet face (25 mm thick post, outlet centre 16 mm from the free end, at x = 0.290) faces the robot's right; the two oxygen pin holes (positions 2 and 5: 4.75 mm, 6 mm deep, with a 0.6 mm 45-degree countersink at the mouth, on a 14.3 mm radius about the outlet centre, 18 degrees either side of the line toward the cylinder) are in that face; a 7 mm conical recess, 2 mm deep, faces the robot's left, opposite the outlet. Cradle (fixed, plywood): two V saddles (each 3 cm wide along x, two 7 x 1.2 cm boards at 45 degrees on a 10 cm wide block, the V's apex 4.4 cm above the table) at x = 0.44 and 0.72, and an upright end board (10 cm wide, 1.2 cm thick, 12.25 cm tall) 1 mm behind the cylinder's base at x = 0.779; the cylinder lies in the saddles under its own weight, nothing straps it. Regulator (yoke type, about 0.39 kg): an aluminium yoke frame 46 mm tall around a 29 x 36 mm window (0.5 mm play above and below the 28 mm post), its 10 mm inlet plate (32 mm along x) carrying a 16 mm black sealing washer (1.6 mm) on the inlet and two steel pins (4 mm, standing 5.5 mm proud, positions 2 and 5); opposite it a 10 mm screw bar with a steel T-screw (8 mm shaft, 5 mm flat tip, 1.75 mm pitch) and a black 60 x 10 mm round T-bar, backed off so the tip is flush with the window's inside; on the inlet side a blue anodised aluminium regulator body, a flat-sided 40 x 65 x 46 mm block (x, y, z), ending in a white 40 mm contents gauge and a 6 mm hose barb. It stands on the table on its frame and body in the orientation it goes on (inlet and pins facing the robot's left, T-bar along x), its inlet's axis at (0.29, -0.13), 2.3 cm above the table. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Watched every control step (20 Hz). 0 if at any time something unsafe happens: the cylinder tips out of its cradle (its axis more than 30 degrees from where it lay, or more than 2 cm below its cradled height); or the regulator is dropped (it moves down faster than 0.5 m/s while no gripper holds it) or falls off the table. Setting the regulator down to regrip it, and sliding or rolling the cylinder in its cradle, are allowed. Otherwise, from the state at the end of the trial, judged relative to the cylinder wherever it lies: 0.25 if the yoke is over the valve post (the post through its window, the yoke's whole 32 mm depth over the post); 0.5 if it is also seated: both pins at least 3 mm into their holes (from a pen mark on each pin; seated fully they reach 3.9 mm), the washer within 1 mm of the outlet face all round (feeler gauge) and the inlet's axis within 3 degrees of the outlet's (the yoke square on the valve face); 0.75 if it is also hand-tight: the screw tip in the recess (within 1.2 mm of its centre) and the T-handle tight enough that a torque gauge on the T-bar reads at least 0.75 N m before it turns further. 1.0 (success): seated and hand-tight, every part of both arms at least 3 cm from the regulator, and the regulator still (it moved less than 1 mm and 0.5 degrees over the last second), held for 1 s with no violation. Doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0.
reset_notes: Unscrew the T-handle until its tip is flush with the inside of the yoke's window (about 6.6 turns, T-bar along x), slide the regulator off and stand it back at its start. Check the cylinder sits in both saddles against the end board. Real trials use an empty cylinder with its valve closed (or a valve on an empty, decommissioned cylinder), so no gas is ever released.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz. Post, pin holes, pins, washer, yoke window and recess are colliders at ISO 407 sizes; round holes (0.6 mm countersink) and the cone recess are square pockets. PhysX has no screw joint: the T-screw is a turn joint on a slide joint, coupled every control step at 1.75 mm per turn, with the clamp force capped at 60 N. Turning resistance rises with clamp force, as damping sized to give 0.75 N m at 28 N and 1.55 N m at 60 N at 100 deg/s. The cylinder lies loose in its cradle.
